Actual recordings · actual feedback

What your examples contain.

We retrieved short excerpts from your three YouTube references and reviewed a bounded sample of their comments. Everything was downloaded and analyzed locally, with no paid AI API.

The most useful product signal is variation between listeners. In the migraine recording’s comments, water sounds are comforting to some and unwanted by others. A personal comfort tool should learn which layers to keep, which to soften, and when the listener wants silence.

These are design hypotheses. Neither a frequency measurement, a view count nor a positive comment establishes treatment efficacy.

Measured audio excerpts

Downloaded with yt-dlp; decoded locally at 44.1 kHz, stereo. These measurements describe short excerpts, not the full recordings or their health effects.

Peaks are listed by spectral power. Welch-style averaging used 131,072-sample Hann windows with 50% overlap (0.336 Hz bin spacing). Sub-bin interpolation is an estimate, not guaranteed resolving power. Spectral centroid depends on this power-weighted definition. Digital levels are not calibrated headphone loudness. Separate tone peaks are not proof of a binaural beat; the signal delivered to each ear must be considered.

First recording: the excerpt has stable tone pairs at approximately 171.5 Hz left / 168.5 Hz right (3.0 Hz apart) and 82.5 Hz left / 82.0 Hz right (about 0.5 Hz apart). Band-specific tracking and a full-excerpt spectrum confirm both pairs; alternating dominant peaks were not treated as a beat. This is compatible with binaural stimulation, but says nothing about whether it reduces migraine pain.

The handpan and singing bowls: these are multi-tone, changing recordings. Their acoustic profiles differ from the first reference. No binaural-beat frequency is inferred by subtracting arbitrary left/right peaks, and neither a title nor a peak establishes a healing effect.

All excerpts decoded to 30.0 seconds. No decoded sample reached digital full scale; this does not establish a safe or comfortable headphone level.

What the sampled comments add

We read 100 top and 100 recent top-level comments from each video: 600 retrieved rows, 557 distinct comment IDs. Three were pinned promotional posts, leaving 554 other comments. The 557 IDs contain 546 distinct exact texts; comments are not verified unique people.

ReferenceTop / recent / distinctUseful observations
Migraine / binaural100 / 100 / 190Repeat-use, relief, sleep and community reassurance appear. Preferences conflict: one listener wants repeated water sounds; another wants no water. Recent comments also report no benefit, nausea, and an opening ping hurting at maximum volume.
Handpan100 / 100 / 176Relaxation, study/work focus and sleep recur. Some mention headache relief or listening after an episode. Another expected calm but cried; this does not by itself mean harm. Comments also question the title’s frequency label.
Singing bowls100 / 100 / 191Listeners value calm, sleep and uninterrupted listening. Recent counterexamples describe annoyance at volume changes, fear and nightmares. Such reports do not establish that the audio caused these experiences.

Product implications to test: separate water/tonal controls; gentle starts and stable levels; dim, low-interaction listening; feedback for discomfort and early stopping; and questions about focus, sleep and emotional response as well as pain.

This is a qualitative convenience sample, not an efficacy estimate. Top and recent lists overlap (10, 24 and 9 IDs respectively). Pinned posts, generic praise and promotional content were present. Diagnoses, medication use and outcomes are unverified. We did not calculate a success rate or turn these comments into treatment labels. Checked 4 November 2026.

How this should change the next POC

  1. Separate the layers. Let listeners compare tones, water/noise, and combinations. Keep carrier pitch and left/right difference as separate controls. No frequency is presented as a medical dose.
  2. Ask about this moment. Record comfort, sound sensitivity and listening purpose; preserve negative responses and early stopping. Keep sleep, focus and pain outcomes separate.
  3. Compare like with like. To investigate the first reference, a future controlled experiment can compare matched tone mixtures with and without ear-specific differences. Change one factor at a time and retain usual care.
  4. Use comments for research questions. These comments are not a training set of verified treatment outcomes. Recruit consenting users and collect structured repeated observations before evaluating personalization.

What was done—and what remains

Retrieval used yt-dlp 2026.10.26. The audio format was YouTube’s stereo AAC stream, decoded locally with FFmpeg; frequency analysis used NumPy. We requested 32:48–33:18 for the first reference and 01:00–01:30 for each of the other two. These short windows may omit other sections, textures or changes in the recordings.

Comment sampling requested 100 top and 100 recent top-level comments for each video, without replies. Review was qualitative, including multilingual comments; it was not independently coded or randomized. Deduplication used comment IDs, with repeated exact text also checked. We retained counts and paraphrased observations, without publishing authors or raw comment dumps.

The live app still uses its original three procedural sound recipes and a simple feedback rule. This follow-up adds evidence; it does not silently turn the app into a trained model or replace its illustrative 6 Hz stereo default with a medically validated setting. Original source audio is not hosted by the app.

Audio analysis, procedural sound generation and local ratings in Still use no paid AI API and require no API key. ChatGPT sign-in controls access to the private site.
